cves.description: When SNMP is configured on the F5OS-A or F5OS-C system, undisclosed requests can cause an increase in SNMP memory resource utilization. (CVE-2025-47150)
cves.impact: System performance can degrade until the SNMP process is either forced to restart or is manually restarted. This vulnerability allows a remote, authenticated attacker to cause a degradation of service that can lead to a denial-of-service (DoS) on the F5OS system. For F5OS Appliance rSeries systems, the system may reboot and affect the availability of running BIG-IP VE or BIG-IP NEXT tenants. For F5OS Chassis Controller and Partitions on F5 VELOS systems, the systems may reboot; however, BIG-IP VE or BIG-IP NEXT tenants are not affected. This is a control plane issue only.
cves.mitigation:
As this attack is conducted by legitimate, authenticated F5OS SNMP users, there is no viable mitigation that also allows SNMP access to the F5OS system. The only mitigation is to remove access for F5OS SNMP users who are not completely trusted. Expose the F5OS management interface to only trusted networks.

F5OS-A

The excess memory used can be released by restarting the snmpd and system_platform-stats-bridge services in the F5OS-A system. Depending on the F5OS-A version running on your rSeries system, perform one of the following procedures:

F5OS-A 1.5.x
F5OS-A 1.8.x

F5OS-A 1.5.x

Log in to the F5OS-A command line as the root user.
Restart the affected services using the following commands:

docker restart snmpd
docker restart system_platform-stats-bridge

F5OS-A 1.8.x

Log in to the F5OS-A command line as the admin user or a user assigned with the admin role.
Change to config mode by entering the following command:

config

Restart the affected services using the following commands:

system diagnostics os-utils docker restart node platform service snmpd
system diagnostics os-utils docker restart node platform service system_platform-stats-bridge

F5OS-C

For F5OS-C active and standby system controllers, restart the snmpd and platform-stats-bridge-cc services. For F5OS-C partitions, restart the partition<n>_snmpd and partition<n>_platform-stats-bridge services where <n> is the partition ID. Perform the following procedures:

F5OS-C 1.6.x

F5OS-C 1.6.x

Log in to the F5OS-C system controller command line as the root user.
Restart the affected services using the following commands:

For system controller,

docker restart snmpd
docker restart platform-stats-bridge-cc

For partition,

docker restart partition<n>_snmpd
docker restart partition<n>_platform-stats-bridge

Note: <n> is the partition ID.

cves.description: An HTTP/2 implementation flaw allows a denial-of-service (DoS) that uses malformed HTTP/2 control frames to break the maximum concurrent streams limit (HTTP/2 MadeYouReset Attack). (CVE-2025-54500)
cves.impact: This vulnerability allows a remote, unauthenticated attacker to cause an increase in CPU usage that can lead to a degradation of service to some users of the BIG-IP system.
cves.mitigation:
BIG-IP and BIG-IP Next

To mitigate this issue for systems and configurations that are able to use either HTTP or HTTP/2, F5 recommends using HTTP and disabling HTTP/2.

For Single CPU BIG-IP VE, small vCMP guests, and F5OS tenant deployments, consider increasing the number of CPU cores to increase capacity of handling crypto transactions and adjust the per-TMM crypto limit. For more information, refer to K000150313: Connection error: per-tmm crypto request limit reached.

BIG-IP Next SPK, BIG-IP Next CNF, and BIG-IP Next for Kubernetes

To mitigate this vulnerability, where possible, you can delete the F5SPKIngressHTTP2 Custom Resource. For more information, refer to the F5SPKIngressHTTP2 CR page and the documentation for your product on F5 Cloud Docs.

BIG-IP ASM and Advanced WAF

To mitigate this vulnerability, you can create a BIG-IP ASM/Advanced WAF DoS protection profile configured with TPS and stress-based attributes, including Behavioral DoS Detection and Mitigation, and associate the BIG-IP ASM/Advanced WAF DoS protection profile with the HTTP/2 virtual server. For TPS and stress-based thresholds and mitigation, set appropriate Relative and Absolute Thresholds and appropriate mitigations for your environment. Note that Stress-based Detection detects and mitigates per server stress. Behavioral DoS Detection needs to observe traffic patterns and server stress under normal conditions in order to detect changes, so you must enable Behavioral DoS Detection before changes in the normal traffic pattern occur.

Indicators of attack for BIG-IP systems

For BIG-IP systems, you can inspect the HTTP/2 profile statistics. If the number of RST_STREAM frames Sent and WINDOW_UPDATE frames Received significantly exceeds the number of other frames received from clients, this may indicate that a malicious actor is conducting this type of attack. If there is no impact on the CPU load of the BIG-IP system, you may not need to take remedial action; however, if a significant or troublesome increase in CPU load is observed, download and install the engineering hotfix for this issue. For information about how to view the HTTP/2 profile statistics using the Configuration utility, tmsh, or SNMP, refer to K000137190: Overview of HTTP/2 Statistics.

cves.mitigation:
To mitigate this vulnerability, you can disable the hardware SYN cookies in the HSB and compute them in software within the TMM. To do so, perform the following procedure.

Impact of action: Performing the following procedure should not have a negative impact on your system.

Log in to the TMOS Shell (tmsh) using the following command:

tmsh
To disable the global hardware VLAN SYN cookie protection on the BIG-IP system, enter the following command:

modify ltm global-settings connection vlan-syn-cookie disabled
To disable TCP and FastL4 profile controls for hardware SYN cookie protection, enter the following command:

modify sys db pvasyncookies.enabled value false

For more information, refer to K74451051: Configuring SYN cookie protection (13.x - 17.x).

Security Advisory Recommended Actions

If you are running a version listed in the Versions known to be vulnerable column, you can eliminate this vulnerability by installing a version listed in the Fixes introduced in column and enabling the tm.tcpstopblindinjection database variable. If the Fixes introduced in column does not list a version for your branch, then no update candidate currently exists for that branch and F5 recommends that you upgrade to a version with the fix (refer to the tables) and enable the tm.tcpstopblindinjection database variable.

If the Fixes introduced in column lists a version prior to the one you are running, in the same branch, then your version should have the fix, however, you still need to enable the tm.tcpstopblindinjection database variable to mitigate the issue.

Mitigation

To mitigate this issue, in addition to installing a fixed version, you must also enable the tm.tcpstopblindinjection database variable. This database variable implements Request for Comment 5961 (RFC5961) section 5 protection but is disabled by default. To enable the database variable, perform the following procedure:

Impact of action: Enabling the tm.tcpstopblindinjection database variable may slightly increase latency and CPU usage on Traffic Management Microkernel (TMM) during typical traffic levels but could further increase under high connection rates or heavy traffic flow.

Important: F5 Product Engineering has identified an issue that affects some connection types like SMTP where the server side sends data first, causing the server data to be dropped. F5 has assigned ID 2132165 to this issue. If you experience connection issues after enabling this DB key, F5 recommends disabling it until the fix is available.

Log in to the TMOS Shell (tmsh) by entering the following command from the Advanced Shell (bash):


tmsh

To enable the tm.tcpstopblindinjection database variable, enter the following command:


modify /sys db tm.tcpstopblindinjection value enable

Verify the change by entering the following command:

list /sys db tm.tcpstopblindinjection

Output should appear similar to the following example:

sys db tm.tcpstopblindinjection {
value "enable" }

To further mitigate this vulnerability for affected F5 products, you should ensure TCP connections in the data plane are protected using protocols that provide message integrity, such as TLS. For more information about securing data plane traffic, refer to the following articles:

K000133414: Best practices for maintaining secure SSL/TLS deployments
K01770517: Configuring the cipher strength for SSL profiles (14.x - 17.x)
K14783: Overview of the Client SSL profile (11.x - 17.x)
K14806: Overview of the Server SSL profile (11.x - 17.x)

cves.mitigation:
Until you can install a fixed version, you can use the following sections as temporary mitigations. These mitigations restrict access to the Configuration utility to only trusted networks or devices, thereby limiting the attack surface.

Block Configuration utility access through self IP addresses
Block Configuration utility access through the management interface

Block Configuration utility access through self IP addresses

You can block all access to the Configuration utility of your BIG-IP system using self IP addresses. To do so, you can change the Port Lockdown setting to Allow None for each self IP address on the system. If you must open any ports, you should use the Allow Custom option, taking care to block access to the Configuration utility. By default, the Configuration utility listens on TCP port 443. If you modified the default port, ensure that you block access to the alternate port you configured.

Note: Performing this action prevents all access to the Configuration utility and iControl REST using the self IP address. These changes may also impact other services, including breaking high availability (HA) configurations. For more information, refer to K46122561: Restrict access to the BIG-IP management interface using network firewall rules.

Before you make changes to the configuration of your self IP addresses, F5 strongly recommends that you refer to the following articles:

K17333: Overview of port lockdown behavior (12.x - 17.x)
K13092: Overview of securing access to the BIG-IP system
K31003634: The Configuration utility of the Single-NIC BIG-IP Virtual Edition now defaults to TCP port 8443
K51358480: The single-NIC BIG-IP VE may erroneously revert to the default management httpd port after a configuration reload

If you must expose port 443 on your self IP addresses and want to restrict access to specific IP ranges, you may consider using the packet filtering functionality built into the BIG-IP system. For more information, refer to the following article:

K13383: Configure CIDR Network Addresses for the BIG-IP packet filter

cves.description: A vulnerability exists in an undisclosed iControl REST and BIG-IP TMOS Shell (tmsh) command that may allow an authenticated attacker with at least the resource administrator role to execute arbitrary system commands with higher privileges. A successful exploit can allow the attacker to cross a security boundary. (CVE-2025-59481)
cves.impact:
In standard deployments, this vulnerability may allow an authenticated attacker with at least resource administrator role privileges and network access to the affected iControl REST endpoint and local access to the affected tmsh command to execute arbitrary system commands with higher privileges and create or delete files through the BIG-IP management port or self IP addresses.

The vulnerability allows the bypass of Appliance mode security on BIG-IP systems by allowing the authenticated attacker with at least resource administrator role privileges to execute arbitrary Advanced Shell (bash) commands with higher privileges. There is no data plane exposure; this is a control plane issue only. There is no Availability impact beyond existing user capabilities.

Note: Appliance mode is enforced by a specific license or may be enabled or disabled for individual Virtual Clustered Multiprocessing (vCMP) guest instances. For more information about Appliance mode, refer to K12815: Overview of Appliance mode.
cves.mitigation:
As this attack is conducted by legitimate, authenticated, administrator role users, there is no viable mitigation that also allows users access to the BIG-IP system. The only mitigation is to remove access for users who are not completely trusted.

Until it is possible to install a fixed version, you can use the following sections as temporary mitigations. These mitigations restrict access to iControl REST to only trusted networks or devices, and to the BIG-IP command line through SSH to only trusted networks or devices, thereby limiting the attack surface.

Block iControl REST access through the self IP address
Block iControl REST access through the management interface
Block SSH access through self IP addresses
Block SSH access through the management interface

Block iControl REST access through the self IP address

You can block all access to the iControl REST interface of your BIG-IP system through self IP addresses. To do so, you can change the Port Lockdown setting to Allow None for each self IP address in the system. If you must open any ports, you should use the Allow Custom option, taking care to disallow access to iControl REST. By default, iControl REST listens on TCP port 443 or TCP port 8443 on single NIC BIG-IP VE instances. If you modified the default port, ensure that you disallow access to the alternate port you configured.

Note: Performing this action prevents all access to the Configuration utility and iControl REST using the self IP address. These changes may also impact other services, including breaking high availability (HA) configurations.

Before you make changes to the configuration of your self IP addresses, F5 strongly recommends that you refer to the following articles:

K17333: Overview of port lockdown behavior (12.x - 17.x)
K13092: Overview of securing access to the BIG-IP system
K31003634: The Configuration utility of the Single-NIC BIG-IP Virtual Edition now defaults to TCP port 8443
K51358480: The single-NIC BIG-IP VE may erroneously revert to the default management httpd port after a configuration reload

If you must expose port 443 on your self IP addresses and want to restrict access to specific IP ranges, you may consider using the packet filtering functionality built into the BIG-IP system. For more information, refer to the following article:

K13383: Configure CIDR Network Addresses for the BIG-IP packet filter

Block iControl REST access through the management interface

To mitigate this vulnerability for affected F5 products, you should restrict management access to only trusted users and devices over a secure network. For more information about securing access to BIG-IP systems, refer to the following articles:

K13092: Overview of securing access to the BIG-IP system
K46122561: Restrict access to the BIG-IP management interface using network firewall rules
K69354049: Use iptables to restrict access to the BIG-IP management interface for Configuration utility and iControl REST services

Block SSH access through self IP addresses

You can block all access to the command line through SSH of your BIG-IP system using self IP addresses. To do so, you can change the Port Lockdown setting to Allow None for each self IP address on the system. If you must open any ports, you should use the Allow Custom option, taking care to block access to SSH. By default, the SSH service listens on TCP port 22.

Note: Performing this action prevents all access to SSH using the self IP address. These changes may also impact other services.

Before you make changes to the configuration of your self IP addresses, F5 strongly recommends that you refer to the following articles:

K17333: Overview of port lockdown behavior (12.x - 17.x)
K13092: Overview of securing access to the BIG-IP system

If you must expose port 22 on your self IP addresses and want to restrict access to specific IP ranges, you may consider using the packet filtering functionality built into the BIG-IP system. For more information, refer to the following article:

K13383: Configure CIDR Network Addresses for the BIG-IP packet filter

Block SSH access through the management interface

To mitigate this vulnerability for affected F5 products, you should restrict management access to F5 products to only trusted users and devices over a secure network. For more information about securing access to BIG-IP systems, refer to the following articles:

K13092: Overview of securing access to the BIG-IP system

cves.description: When Diffie-Hellman (DH) group Elliptic Curve Cryptography (ECC) Brainpool curves are configured in an SSL profile's Cipher Rule or Cipher Group, and that profile is applied to a virtual server, undisclosed traffic can cause the Traffic Management Microkernel (TMM) to terminate. (CVE-2025-60016)
cves.impact:
Traffic is disrupted while the TMM process restarts. This vulnerability allows a remote, unauthenticated attacker to cause a denial-of-service (DoS) on the BIG-IP system. There is no control plane exposure; this is a data plane issue only.

Note: This issue affects both Client SSL and Server SSL profiles, as long as they are configured with a Cipher Rule or Cipher Group that includes an ECC Brainpool curve in the DH Groups setting.
cves.mitigation:
To mitigate this vulnerability, ensure that ECC Brainpool curves are not selected in the DH Groups setting of the Cipher Rule or Cipher Group associated with the affected SSL profile.

To verify if ECC Brainpool curves are used in any of the cipher rules, review the Local Traffic > Ciphers > Rules page in the BIG-IP Configuration utility.

Alternatively, you can use the following TMOS Shell (tmsh) command to determine if any of the cipher rules are using ECC Brainpool curves:

tmsh
cd /
list ltm cipher rule recursive one-line | grep BRA

If there are cipher rules using ECC Brainpool curves, then you may observe an output similar to the following example:

ltm cipher rule K000137488-rule { cipher DEFAULT description "Elliptic Curve Cryptography Brainpool curves" dh-groups BRAINPOOLP256R1:BRAINPOOLP384R1:BRAINPOOLP256R1TLS13:BRAINPOOLP384R1TLS13 signature-algorithms DEFAULT }

As of version 17.1.0, BIG-IP supports ECC Brainpool curves. For more information, refer to K000137488: How to implement Elliptic Curve Cryptography Brainpool curves in BIG-IP 17.1.x.

To remove ECC Brainpool curves from the affected cipher rule, perform either of the following procedures:

Impact of action: Performing the following procedure should not have a negative impact on your system.

Configuration utility

Log in to the Configuration utility.
Go to Local Traffic > Ciphers > Rules.
Select the name of the affected cipher rule.
Remove the ECC Brainpool curves definition from the DH Groups setting.
Select Update to save the change.

tmsh utility

Log in to the tmsh utility.
Remove the ECC Brainpool curves definition from the dh-groups setting by entering the following tmsh command syntax:

modify /ltm cipher rule <name of cipher rule> dh-groups <none | other Elliptic Curve Diffie-Hellman key exchange algorithms excluding the Brainpool curves>

Save the change by entering the following tmsh command:

save /sys config

Verify the change by entering the following tmsh command syntax:

list /ltm cipher rule <name of cipher rule>

affected.vulnerable_component: Data Guard Protection Enforcement URL/the bd process

cves.description: When a BIG-IP Advanced WAF or ASM security policy is configured with a URL greater than 1024 characters in length for the Data Guard Protection Enforcement setting, either manually or through the automatic Policy Builder, the bd process can terminate repeatedly. (CVE-2025-61938)
cves.impact: Traffic is disrupted while the bd process restarts. This vulnerability allows a remote, unauthenticated attacker to use the automatic Policy Builder to trigger a long Data Guard Protection Enforcement URL configuration for the security policy and cause a denial-of-service (DoS) on the affected BIG-IP Advanced WAF or ASM system. Automatic Policy Builder will learn a URL only if it receives a valid HTTP response when requested. There is no control plane exposure; this is a data plane issue only.
cves.mitigation:
To mitigate this vulnerability, you can replace the long URL in the Data Guard Protection Enforcement setting with a wildcard URL. To do so, perform the following procedure:

Impact of action: Performing the following procedure should not have a negative impact on your system.

Log in to the Configuration utility of the affected BIG-IP Advanced WAF/ASM system as the administrative user.
Go to Security > Application Security > Security Policies > Policies List.
Select the affected security policy.
Select Advanced Protection.
Select Data Guard.
Locate the long URL and select x to remove it.
To replace the long URL, enter a wildcard URL and select Add.
Select Save.
Select Apply Policy.

For more information about the Data Guard feature, refer to the Protecting Sensitive Data with Data Guard chapter of the BIG-IP Application Security Manager: Implementations manual.

cves.description: The 32-bit implementation of NGINX Open Source has a vulnerability in the ngx_http_mp4_module module, which might allow an attacker to over-read or over-write NGINX worker memory resulting in its termination, using a specially crafted MP4 file. The issue only affects 32-bit NGINX Open Source if it is built with the ngx_http_mp4_module module and the mp4 directive is used in the configuration file. Additionally, the attack is possible only if an attacker can trigger the processing of a specially crafted MP4 file with the ngx_http_mp4_module module. (CVE-2026-27784)
cves.impact:
Traffic is disrupted while the NGINX worker process restarts. This vulnerability allows a local, authenticated attacker to cause a denial-of-service (DoS) of the NGINX system. There is no control plane exposure; this is a data plane issue only.

Note: The MP4 module is not included by default and must be explicitly enabled for NGINX Open Source edition. The MP4 module is included in NGINX Plus.
cves.mitigation:
To mitigate this vulnerability for affected products, restrict publishing of audio and video files to trusted users only. Optionally, you can disable the MP4 module in your NGINX configuration until you can update your product version. To do so, perform the following procedure:

Impact of action: The following procedure disables the server-side pseudo-streaming support for MP4 files provided by this module. F5 recommends that you test these changes during a maintenance window and consider the possible impact on your specific environment.

Log in to the command line of your NGINX host system with administrative privileges.
Change directories to your NGINX configuration directory, usually in /etc/nginx.

Note: The configuration can be stubbed out to multiple files, so be sure to review all appropriate configuration sections.

Using your preferred text editor, locate all configuration blocks containing mp4 directives and enter a hash character (#) at the beginning of the line to comment out the directive. For example:

Note: If there are multiple configuration blocks with mp4 directives, F5 recommends that you test changes one at a time. Additionally, mp4 directives are supported in the http, server, and location contexts.

location /video/ {
    # mp4;
    # mp4_buffer_size       1m;
    # mp4_max_buffer_size   5m;
    # mp4_limit_rate         on;
    # mp4_limit_rate_after   30s;
}

Save your changes and exit the text editor.
Test the configuration changes by entering the following command:

sudo nginx -t

Output should appear similar to the following example:

nginx: the configuration file /etc/nginx/nginx.conf syntax is ok
nginx: configuration file /etc/nginx/nginx.conf test is successful

Reload the NGINX configuration by entering the following command:

sudo service nginx reload

For more information about configuration options for the ngx_http_mp4_module module, refer to the Module ngx_http_mp4_module page.

cves.description: NGINX Open Source and NGINX Plus have a vulnerability in the ngx_http_mp4_module module, which might allow an attacker to trigger a buffer over-read or over-write to the NGINX worker memory resulting in its termination or possibly code execution, using a specially crafted MP4 file. This issue affects NGINX Open Source and NGINX Plus if it is built with the ngx_http_mp4_module module and the mp4 directive is used in the configuration file. Additionally, the attack is possible only if an attacker can trigger the processing of a specially crafted MP4 file with the ngx_http_mp4_module module. (CVE-2026-32647)
cves.impact:
Traffic is disrupted while the NGINX worker process restarts. This vulnerability allows a local, authenticated attacker to cause a denial-of-service (DoS) of the NGINX system or to possibly trigger a code execution. There is no control plane exposure; this is a data plane issue only.

Note: The MP4 module is not included by default and must be explicitly enabled for NGINX Open Source edition. The MP4 module is included in NGINX Plus.
cves.mitigation:
To mitigate this vulnerability for affected products, restrict publishing of audio and video files to trusted users only. Optionally, you can disable the MP4 module in your NGINX configuration until you can update your product version. To do so, perform the following procedure:

Impact of action: The following procedure disables the server-side pseudo-streaming support for MP4 files provided by this module. F5 recommends that you test these changes during a maintenance window and consider the possible impact on your specific environment.

Log in to the command line of your NGINX host system with administrative privileges.
Change directories to your NGINX configuration directory, usually in /etc/nginx.

Note: The configuration can be stubbed out to multiple files, so be sure to review all appropriate configuration sections.

Using your preferred text editor, locate all configuration blocks containing mp4 directives and enter a hash character (#) at the beginning of the line to comment out the directive. For example:

Note: If there are multiple configuration blocks with mp4 directives, F5 recommends that you test changes one at a time. Additionally, mp4 directives are supported in the http, server, and location contexts.

location /video/ {
# mp4;
# mp4_buffer_size 1m;
# mp4_max_buffer_size 5m;
# mp4_limit_rate on;
# mp4_limit_rate_after 30s;
}

Save your changes and exit the text editor.
Test the configuration changes by entering the following command:

sudo nginx -t

Output should appear similar to the following example:

nginx: the configuration file /etc/nginx/nginx.conf syntax is ok
nginx: configuration file /etc/nginx/nginx.conf test is successful

Reload the NGINX configuration by entering the following command:

sudo service nginx reload

For more information about configuration options for the ngx_http_mp4_module module, refer to the Module ngx_http_mp4_module page.

cves.description: A vulnerability exists in BIG-IP scripted monitors that may allow an authenticated attacker with the Resource Administrator or Administrator role to execute arbitrary system commands with higher privileges. In appliance mode deployments, a successful exploit can allow the attacker to cross a security boundary. (CVE-2026-32673)
cves.impact:
In standard deployments, this vulnerability may allow an authenticated attacker with Resource Administrator or Administrator role privileges and network access to the affected iControl REST endpoint or local access to the affected TMOS Shell (tmsh) command to execute arbitrary system commands with higher privileges and create or delete files through the BIG-IP management port or self IP addresses.

The vulnerability allows the bypass of Appliance mode security on BIG-IP systems by allowing the authenticated attacker with Resource Administrator or Administrator role privileges to execute arbitrary Advanced Shell (bash) commands with higher privileges. There is no data plane exposure; this is a control plane issue only. There is no Availability impact beyond existing user capabilities.

Note: Appliance mode is enforced by a specific license or may be enabled or disabled for individual Virtual Clustered Multiprocessing (vCMP) guest instances. For more information about Appliance mode, refer to K12815: Overview of Appliance mode.

As this attack is conducted by legitimate, authenticated Resource Administrator and Administrator role users, there is no viable mitigation that also allows users access to the BIG-IP system. The only mitigation is to remove access for users who are not completely trusted.

The vulnerability allows the bypass of Appliance mode security on BIG-IP systems by allowing the authenticated attacker with Resource Administrator or Administrator role privileges to execute arbitrary Advanced Shell (bash) commands with higher privileges. There is no data plane exposure; this is a control plane issue only. There is no availability impact beyond existing user capabilities.

Note: Appliance mode is enforced by a specific license or may be enabled or disabled for individual Virtual Clustered Multiprocessing (vCMP) guest instances. For more information about Appliance mode, refer to K12815: Overview of Appliance mode.
cves.mitigation:
As this attack is conducted by legitimate, authenticated, Resource Administrator or Administrator role users, there is no viable mitigation that also allows users access to the BIG-IP system. The only mitigation is to remove access for users who are not completely trusted.

Until it is possible to install a fixed version, you can use the following sections as temporary mitigations. These mitigations restrict access to iControl REST to only trusted networks or devices, and to the BIG-IP command line through SSH to only trusted networks or devices, thereby limiting the attack surface.

Block iControl REST access through the self IP address
Block iControl REST access through the management interface
Block SSH access through self IP addresses
Block SSH access through the management interface

Block iControl REST access through the self IP address

You can block all access to the iControl REST interface of your BIG-IP system through self IP addresses. To do so, you can change the Port Lockdown setting to Allow None for each self IP address in the system. If you must open any ports, you should use the Allow Custom option, taking care to disallow access to iControl REST. By default, iControl REST listens on TCP port 443 or TCP port 8443 on single NIC BIG-IP VE instances. If you modified the default port, ensure that you disallow access to the alternate port you configured.

Note: Performing this action prevents all access to the Configuration utility and iControl REST using the self IP address. These changes may also impact other services, including breaking high availability (HA) configurations.

Before you make changes to the configuration of your self IP addresses, F5 strongly recommends that you refer to the following articles:

K17333: Overview of port lockdown behavior (12.x - 21.x)
K13092: Overview of securing access to the BIG-IP system
K31003634: The Configuration utility of the Single-NIC BIG-IP Virtual Edition now defaults to TCP port 8443
K51358480: The single-NIC BIG-IP VE may erroneously revert to the default management httpd port after a configuration reload

If you must expose port 443 on your self IP addresses and want to restrict access to specific IP ranges, you may consider using the packet filtering functionality built into the BIG-IP system. For more information, refer to the following article:

K13383: Configure CIDR Network Addresses for the BIG-IP packet filter

Block iControl REST access through the management interface

To mitigate this vulnerability for affected F5 products, you should restrict management access to only trusted users and devices over a secure network. For more information about securing access to BIG-IP systems, refer to the following articles:

K13092: Overview of securing access to the BIG-IP system
K46122561: Restrict access to the BIG-IP management interface using network firewall rules
K69354049: Use iptables to restrict access to the BIG-IP management interface for Configuration utility and iControl REST services

Block SSH access through self IP addresses

You can block all access to the command line through SSH of your BIG-IP system using self IP addresses. To do so, you can change the Port Lockdown setting to Allow None for each self IP address on the system. If you must open any ports, you should use the Allow Custom option, taking care to block access to SSH. By default, the SSH service listens on TCP port 22.

Note: Performing this action prevents all access to SSH using the self IP address. These changes may also impact other services.

Before you make changes to the configuration of your self IP addresses, F5 strongly recommends that you refer to the following articles:

K17333: Overview of port lockdown behavior (12.x - 21.x)
K13092: Overview of securing access to the BIG-IP system

If you must expose port 22 on your self IP addresses and want to restrict access to specific IP ranges, you may consider using the packet filtering functionality built into the BIG-IP system. For more information, refer to the following article:

K13383: Configure CIDR Network Addresses for the BIG-IP packet filter

Block SSH access through the management interface

To mitigate this vulnerability for affected F5 products, you should restrict management access to F5 products to only trusted users and devices over a secure network. For more information about securing access to BIG-IP systems, refer to the following articles:

K13092: Overview of securing access to the BIG-IP system

cves.description: When SSL profiles are configured on a virtual server, undisclosed traffic can cause the virtual server to stop processing new client connections. (CVE-2026-40629)
cves.impact: Traffic is disrupted for new client connections. This vulnerability allows a remote, unauthenticated attacker to cause a denial-of-service (DoS) on the BIG-IP system, specific to the impacted virtual server. There is no control plane exposure; this is a data plane issue only.
cves.mitigation:
BIG-IP

To mitigate this vulnerability, you can reduce the Alert Timeout value in the affected client SSL profile. To do so, perform the following procedure:

Impact of action: With a lower alert timeout, the BIG-IP system may terminate SSL sessions more quickly if a client is slow to send its close_notify. As a result, some SSL connections may be dropped prematurely in high-latency environments or under load. F5 recommends testing this in a staging environment first and monitoring the /var/log/ltm logs for messages.

Log in to the Configuration utility.
Go to Local Traffic > Profiles > SSL > Client SSL.
Select the name of the profile associated with the virtual server.
Next to Configuration, select Advanced.
For Alert Timeout, select Specify.
Enter a low value. For example, you can start with 1 second.
Select Update.

cves.description: NGINX Plus and NGINX Open Source have a vulnerability in the ngx_http_ssl_module module when the ssl_verify_client directive is set to "on" or "optional," and the ssl_ocsp directive is set to "on" or the leaf parameters are configured with a resolver. With this configuration, an unauthenticated attacker can send requests along with conditions beyond its control that may cause a heap-use-after-free error in the NGINX worker process. This vulnerability may result in limited modification of data or the NGINX worker process restarting. (CVE-2026-40701)
cves.impact: This vulnerability may allow remote attackers to have limited control of modification of data or restart the NGINX worker process. There is no control plane exposure; this is a data plane issue only.
cves.mitigation:
To mitigate this vulnerability, you can specifically set the OCSP responder, using the ssl_ocsp_responder directive. For more information, refer to the ssl_ocsp_responder section of the Module ngx_http_ssl_module page.

If you are not able to specify the OCSP responder, you can limit the impact of this vulnerability by ensuring that the DNS server used by the NGINX system resolves OCSP responder names quickly. To do so, use a local DNS server and cache the host names. This does not fully mitigate the issue but may reduce its probability.

Alternatively, you can switch from using OCSP to using CRL files. The CRL file can be specified using the ssl_crl directive. For more information, refer to the ssl_crl section of the Module ngx_http_ssl_module page.

Note: F5 recommends that you test all modifications prior to deploying in production and that you perform these changes during a maintenance window.

In Appliance mode deployments, a successful exploit can allow the attacker to cross a security boundary. (CVE-2026-41217)
cves.impact:
In standard deployments, this vulnerability may allow an authenticated attacker with resource administrator or administrator role privileges and local access to the affected tmsh command to execute arbitrary system commands with higher privileges and create or delete files through the BIG-IP management port or self IP addresses.

The vulnerability allows the bypass of Appliance mode security on BIG-IP systems by allowing the authenticated attacker with resource administrator or administrator role privileges to execute arbitrary Advanced Shell (bash) commands with higher privileges. There is no data plane exposure; this is a control plane issue only. There is no Availability impact beyond existing user capabilities.

Note: Appliance mode is enforced by a specific license or may be enabled or disabled for individual Virtual Clustered Multiprocessing (vCMP) guest instances. For more information about Appliance mode, refer to K12815: Overview of Appliance mode.

As this attack is conducted by legitimate, authenticated resource administrator or administrator role users, there is no viable mitigation that also allows users access to the BIG-IP system. The only mitigation is to remove access for users who are not completely trusted.

Block iControl REST access through the self IP address

Self IP addresses

tmsh

Remove all IP addresses or ranges of IP addresses from the list of allowed addresses by entering the following command:

modify /sys icontrol-soap allow replace-all-with { }

Save the change by entering the following command:

save /sys config

cves.description: When embedded Packet Velocity Acceleration (ePVA) acceleration is configured, undisclosed local ethernet traffic can cause an increase in ePVA and Traffic Management Microkernel (TMM) resource utilization. (CVE-2026-42781)
cves.impact:
System performance can degrade until the TMM process is either forced to restart or is manually restarted. This vulnerability allows an unauthenticated attacker on the local network to cause a degradation of service that can lead to a denial-of-service (DoS) on the BIG-IP system. There is no control plane exposure; this is a data plane issue only.

Note that only BIG-IP tenants deployed on the following F5 rSeries and VELOS systems with ePVA are affected:

r5000 rSeries
r10000 rSeries
r12000 rSeries
BX110 blades on VELOS
BX520 blades on VELOS

BIG-IP tenants deployed on all other F5 rSeries systems are not affected.
cves.mitigation:
You can mitigate this issue by disabling ePVA acceleration on affected virtual servers; for example, avoid using the fastL4 profile. Alternatively, you can enforce ARP security on the connected network; for example, deploying Dynamic ARP Inspection in your network environment or using static ARP entries. For information about managing static ARP entries on the BIG-IP system, refer to the Address Resolution Protocol chapter of the BIG-IP TMOS: Routing Administration guide.

cves.description: NGINX Plus and NGINX Open Source have a vulnerability in the ngx_http_rewrite_module module. This vulnerability exists when a rewrite directive uses a regex pattern with distinct, overlapping Perl-Compatible Regular Expression (PCRE) captures (for example, ^/((.*))$) and a replacement string that references multiple such captures (for example, $1$2) in a redirect or arguments context. An unauthenticated attacker along with conditions beyond their control can exploit this vulnerability by sending crafted HTTP requests. This may cause a heap buffer overflow in the NGINX worker process leading to a restart. Additionally, attackers can execute code on systems with Address Space Layout Randomization (ASLR) disabled or when the attacker can bypass ASLR. (CVE-2026-9256)
cves.impact: This vulnerability may allow remote attackers to cause a denial-of-service (DoS) on the NGINX system or to possibly trigger a code execution. There is no control plane exposure; this is a data plane issue only.
cves.mitigation:
To mitigate this vulnerability, use named captures instead of unnamed captures in rewrite definitions.

For example, the following rewrite directive uses unnamed PCRE capture groups, $1 and $2:

rewrite ^/users/([0-9]+)/profile/(.*)$ /profile.php?id=$1&tab=$2 last;

To mitigate this vulnerability for this example, replace $1 and $2 with the appropriate named captures, $user_id and $section:

rewrite ^/users/(?<user_id>[0-9]+)/profile/(?<section>.*)$ /profile.php?id=$user_id&tab=$section last;

cves.description:
A specifically crafted HTTP request may lead the BIG-IP system to generate multiple HTTP redirect responses.

This issue occurs when all of the following conditions are met:

A virtual server has one or more of the following configurations:
An iRule with an HTTP::redirect or an HTTP::respond command that redirects HTTP requests based on the content of the request.
An LTM policy that redirects HTTP requests based on the content of the request.
The virtual server receives and processes a malformed HTTP request.
cves.impact: The BIG-IP system may respond with multiple HTTP redirect responses. Intermediate systems may cache these HTTP redirect responses and clients may unexpectedly receive them.
cves.mitigation:
To work around this issue, you can associate the following mitigation iRule to the affected BIG-IP virtual server. The mitigation iRule should be listed as the first iRule on the virtual servers iRule list before the HTTP redirection iRules:

Important: If an LTM policy is redirecting HTTP requests, convert the LTM policy redirect conditions to an iRule with HTTP::redirect syntax.

# F5 iRule for Mitigation of HTTP Redirect Response
# For additional information please see https://my.f5.com/manage/s/article/K000137322
#
# Version 1.0 - 2023-10-26 09:00 Pacific
# - Initial Release
# Version 1.1 - 2023-10-26 14:00 Pacific
# - Added LWS / header continuation detecting

when RULE_INIT {
    # Set debug to 1 for logging actions, 0 to disable logging (recommended in production)
    set static::smuggling_mitigation_logging 0
}

when HTTP_REQUEST priority 1 {
    set contentLength [string trim [HTTP::header "Content-Length"]]
    set requestMethod [HTTP::method]
    set transferEncoding [string tolower [HTTP::header "Transfer-Encoding"]]

    # Check for chunked transfer encoding

    if {$transferEncoding eq "chunked"} {
        if {$static::smuggling_mitigation_logging == 1} {
            log local0. "Chunked Transfer-Encoding detected. Bypassing Content-Length checks."
        }
        unset -nocomplain contentLength requestMethod transferEncoding
        return
    }

    if {($contentLength eq "" || $contentLength < 0) && ([string tolower [HTTP::header names]] contains "content-length")} {
        event disable all
        reject
        if {$static::smuggling_mitigation_logging == 1} {
            log local0. "Blocked request with empty Content-Length"
        }
       return
    }

    if {(![string is double -strict $contentLength] || [string match "*+*" $contentLength] || [string match "*-*" $contentLength] || [string match "*.*"      $contentLength]) && $contentLength ne ""} {
        event disable all
        reject
        if {$static::smuggling_mitigation_logging == 1} {
            log local0. "Blocked request with invalid Content-Length: $contentLength"
        }
        return
    }

    foreach header [HTTP::header names] {
        set header_value [HTTP::header values $header]

        if { (([string tolower $header_value] contains "content-length") ||
        ([string tolower $header_value] contains "transfer-encoding")) &&
        ([string first ":" $header_value] >= 0) } {
            event disable all
            reject
            if {$static::smuggling_mitigation_logging == 1} {
                log local0. "Dropping request from [IP::client_addr] due to presence of suspect header value of $header"
            }
            return
        }
    }

    if {$static::smuggling_mitigation_logging == 1} {
        log local0. "Content-Length: $contentLength"
    }
    unset -nocomplain contentLength requestMethod transferEncoding header header_value
}


BIG-IP

To create the mitigation iRule and associate it with a virtual server, perform the following procedure:

Impact of procedure: Performing this procedure should not have a negative impact on your system.

Log in to the Configuration utility of the affected BIG-IP system.
Go to Local Traffic > iRules > iRule List.
Select Create.
Enter a value for Name. For example, K000137322.
Copy the mitigation iRule and paste it into the Definition box.
Select Finished to save the iRule.
Go to Local Traffic > Virtual Servers > Virtual Server List.
Select the name of the virtual server.
Select Resources.
In the iRules section, select Manage.
Select the iRule you have configured in previous steps from the Available box and move it to the Enabled box by selecting <<.
Continue to select Up to move the new iRule to the top of the list.
Select Finished.

Note: For more information about the priority iRule command, refer to the F5 Cloud Docs priority page.

BIG-IP Next

To create the mitigation iRule and associate it with an application, perform the following procedure:

Impact of procedure: Performing this procedure should not have a negative impact on your system.

Log in to BIG-IP Next Central Manager.
Select Go To Application Workspace.
Select the iRules tab, then select + Create.
Enter a value for Name. For example, K000137322.
Copy the mitigation iRule and paste it into the box, and then select Save.
Go to Applications > My Application Services.
Select an application using an affected redirect iRule.
Select Edit at the top of the page.
Next to the iRules column, select the editing icon.
Select + Add, select the check box next to the newly created mitigation iRule, and then select the Add button.
Select the check box next to the newly added mitigation iRule, select the up arrow at the top of the page to ensure it is in the first row, then select Save.
Select Review & Deploy to confirm the deployment.
Repeat steps 6-12 for each affected application.

Additionally, in BIG-IP 15.1.0 and later, F5 recommends enabling RFC protocol compliance in the HTTP profile. This optional feature helps protect against a wide range of other HTTP smuggling attacks. To do so, select the check box next to the Enforce RFC Compliance setting in your HTTP profile. HTTP profiles are located on the Local Traffic > Profiles > Services > HTTP page. For more information, refer to K40413116: Information about the Enforcement of RFC compliance for the HTTP protocol feature.

cves.description:
BIG-IP Advanced WAF/ASM, BIG-IP Next WAF, or NGINX App Protect WAF may fail to match an attack signature.

This issue occurs when all of the following conditions are met:

The affected security policy has a large number of attack signatures enabled (for example, all or most F5 provided signatures).
A number of custom attack signatures is created and enabled on the affected security policy.
cves.impact:
An attacker may be able to bypass the affected attack signature. As a result, the backend servers protected by the BIG-IP Advanced WAF/ASM, BIG-IP Next WAF, or NGINX App Protect WAF may be exposed to a vulnerability due to the bypassed attack signature.

Symptoms

As a result of this issue, you may encounter the following symptom:

The backend servers protected by the BIG-IP Advanced WAF/ASM, BIG-IP Next WAF, or NGINX App Protect WAF may be exposed to a vulnerability due to the bypassed attack signature.
cves.mitigation:
F5 recommends that you use appropriate signatures for your environment and that you not assign all signatures to your policy unless necessary.

You can check the signature states locally using the command line of the BIG-IP Advanced WAF/ASM system.

BIG-IP Advanced WAF/ASM system Command line

Log in to the BIG-IP Advanced WAF/ASM system as the root user.
Check the signature states locally by entering the following command:

perl -MF5::NegativeSignatures::Collection::Compiler -MData::Dumper -MF5::DbUtils -e '$dbh = F5::DbUtils::get_dbh(); $sigs = $dbh->selectall_arrayref("SELECT sig_id, rule FROM PLC.NEGSIG_SIGNATURES WHERE apply_to = 1 UNION SELECT threat_campaign_id, match_rule FROM PLC.THREAT_CAMPAIGNS_MATCH_RULES WHERE apply_to = 1", { Slice => {} }); $blob = F5::NegativeSignatures::Collection::Compiler::get_compiled_collection(sigs => $sigs); $len = length($blob); $states = unpack("i1", $blob); print "\nsize [$len] num of states [$states] \n";'

The command should return output similar to the following example:

size [1761051] num of states [28862]

If the number of states is greater than or equal to 65535, the system is impacted by this Security Exposure. F5 recommends that you reduce the number of signatures enabled in the policy or upgrade to a fixed release. For information about managing attack signatures on the BIG-IP Advanced WAF/ASM system, refer to the Assigning Attack Signatures to Security Policies chapter of the BIG-IP Application Security Manager: Attack and Bot Signatures guide.

cves.description:
An authenticated attacker granted the guest role on a BIG-IP system can modify the SMTP Server Host Name as well as the SMTP Server Port Number settings and run the Test Connection feature.

This issue occurs when the following condition is met:

The affected BIG-IP system is configured to send mail through an SMTP server and has an existing SMTP configuration on the System > Configuration > Device > SMTP page.

Note: The guest role does not have the permissions to create a new SMTP configuration on the BIG-IP system.
cves.impact:
The authenticated attacker can use the affected BIG-IP system as a port scanner to scan IP addresses that the BIG-IP system can reach and the BIG-IP system can report if the port is open or close.

Symptoms

As a result of this issue, you may encounter the following symptom:

Your backend device(s) may receive port open requests for a wide range of services from the affected BIG-IP system, indicating port scan activity is occurring.
cves.mitigation:
As this attack is conducted by legitimate, authenticated users, there is no viable mitigation that also allows users access to the Configuration utility. The only mitigation is to remove access for users who are not completely trusted.

Until it is possible to install a fixed version, you can use the following sections as temporary mitigations. These mitigations restrict access to the Configuration utility to only trusted networks or devices, thereby limiting the attack surface.

Block Configuration utility access through self IP addresses
Block Configuration utility access through the management interface

Block Configuration utility access through self IP addresses

You can block all access to the Configuration utility of your BIG-IP system using self IP addresses. To do so, you can change the Port Lockdown setting to Allow None for each self IP address on the system. If you must open any ports, you should use the Allow Custom option, taking care to block access to the Configuration utility. By default, the Configuration utility listens on TCP port 443. If you modified the default port, ensure that you block access to the alternate port you configured.

Note: Performing this action prevents all access to the Configuration utility and iControl REST using the self IP address. These changes may also impact other services, including breaking high availability (HA) configurations. For more information, refer to K46122561: Restrict access to the BIG-IP management interface using network firewall rules.

Before you make changes to the configuration of your self IP addresses, F5 strongly recommends that you refer to the following articles:

K17333: Overview of port lockdown behavior (12.x - 17.x)
K13092: Overview of securing access to the BIG-IP system
K31003634: The Configuration utility of the Single-NIC BIG-IP Virtual Edition now defaults to TCP port 8443
K51358480: The single-NIC BIG-IP VE may erroneously revert to the default management httpd port after a configuration reload

If you must expose port 443 on your self IP addresses and want to restrict access to specific IP ranges, you may consider using the packet filtering functionality built into the BIG-IP system. For more information, refer to the following article:

K13383: Configure CIDR Network Addresses for the BIG-IP packet filter

Block Configuration utility access through the management interface

To mitigate this vulnerability for affected F5 products, you should restrict management access to F5 products to only trusted users and devices over a secure network. For more information about securing access to BIG-IP systems, refer to the following articles:

K13309: Restricting access to the Configuration utility by source IP address (11.x - 17.x)
K13092: Overview of securing access to the BIG-IP system
K46122561: Restrict access to the BIG-IP management interface using network firewall rules

cves.description:
This issue occurs when a non-RFC-compliant HTTP request is received by a virtual server on a system matching one of the following conditions:

BIG-IP 15.1.0 and later version with a virtual server with an HTTP profile with Enforce RFC Compliance enabled.
All supported versions of BIG-IP with a virtual server with an ASM/Advanced WAF security policy.
cves.impact:
Non-RFC-compliant HTTP requests are forwarded to the backend pool members.

Symptoms

As a result of this issue, you may encounter the following symptom:

The backend pool member may respond with a 400 Bad Request HTTP status.
cves.mitigation:
None

Important: To provide protection against this issue, after you install the fixed version on BIG-IP systems with Advanced WAF/ASM provisioned, make sure you enable the Unparsable request content sub-violation under the HTTP protocol compliance failed violation in the security policy that is applied to the virtual server. The Unparsable request content sub-violation is enabled, by default, on BIG-IP 14.1.x through 17.1.x. To verify whether the Unparsable request content sub-violation is enabled, complete the following steps:
1. Log in to the BIG-IP Advanced WAF/ASM Configuration utility.
2. Go to Security > Application Security > Policy Building > Learning and Blocking Settings.
3. Select the affected security policy from the policy list setting.
4. To search for the sub-violation, in the Policy Building Settings search box, enter Unparsable request content.

A specifically crafted HTTP request may bypass BIG-IP HTTP RFC enforcement and may lead the BIG-IP system to pass malformed HTTP requests to a target pool member web server.

You are running a BIG-IP version that contains the fix for the issue described in K50375550: A specifically crafted HTTP request may lead the BIG-IP system to pass malformed HTTP requests to a target pool member web server (HTTP Desync Attack)
Depending on your BIG-IP version, you enabled HTTP RFC Compliance by performing one of the following steps:
Select the Enforce RFC Compliance checkbox under the Enforcement section of the HTTP profile for the affected BIG-IP virtual server.
Enable the tmm.http.rfc.enforcement Database Variable and reboot the BIG-IP system.
cves.impact:

As a result of this issue, you may encounter the following symptom:

Depending on the client requests and HTTP RFC compliance of the target pool member web server, the pool member web server may interpret the client requests differently and perform unintended actions.
cves.mitigation:
